paragraphs: Bodily strength, once what distinguished heroes, has now fallen into such undeserved contempt that men and women alike seem to think it unnecessary: women because it detracts from their feminine graces and from that lovely weakness which is the source of their undue power; men because it seems incompatible with the character of a gentleman.

It can easily be shown that both, in moving away from one extreme, have run into the other; but first it may be proper to point out that a common error has gained a degree of acceptance and has lent force to a false conclusion, one in which an effect has been mistaken for a cause.

People of genius have very often damaged their health by study or by careless neglect of it, and because the violence of their passions is proportioned to the vigour of their intellects, the saying that the sword wears out the scabbard has become almost proverbial. From this, superficial observers have concluded that men of genius usually have weak constitutions — or, to use a more fashionable word, delicate ones. Yet I believe the facts will prove the opposite; for, having inquired diligently, I find that in most cases strength of mind has gone together with superior strength of body — a natural soundness of constitution, that is, not the robust nerves and powerful muscles that come from physical labour while the mind lies idle or merely directs the hands.

In the preface to his biographical chart, Dr. Priestley has observed that most great men have lived past forty-five. And considering how thoughtlessly they squandered their strength — wasting the lamp of life in pursuit of a favourite science, forgetful of the midnight hour; or, lost in poetic dreams, letting fancy people the scene until the passions that meditation had stirred disturbed the soul and shook the constitution, while the objects of those passions, the baseless fabric of a vision, faded before the exhausted eye — they must have had frames of iron. Shakespeare did not grasp the airy dagger with a feeble hand, and Milton did not tremble when he led Satan far from the borders of his dreary prison. These were not the ravings of feebleness or the sickly outpourings of disordered brains; they were the overflowing of an imagination that, wandering “in a fine phrenzy,” was not constantly reminded of its material chains.

I know that this argument would take me further than people may suppose I wish to go; but I follow the truth, and, holding to my first position, I will grant that bodily strength seems to give man a natural superiority over woman; and this is the only solid ground on which the superiority of his sex can be built. But I still insist that the two sexes should have not only the same virtue but the same KNOWLEDGE in kind, if not in degree; and that women, regarded as rational as well as moral creatures, should try to acquire human virtues (or perfections) by the SAME means as men, instead of being brought up as a fanciful sort of HALF being, one of Rousseau’s wild chimeras.

But if men can, with some show of reason, boast of their bodily strength, why are women so infatuated as to take pride in a defect? Rousseau has supplied them with a plausible excuse — one that could only have occurred to a man whose imagination had been allowed to run wild and to embroider the impressions made on his exquisite senses — so that they might, forsooth, have a pretext for yielding to a natural appetite without violating a romantic kind of modesty that flatters the pride and libertinism of man.

Misled by these sentiments, women sometimes boast of their weakness, and cunningly gain power by playing on the WEAKNESS of men; and well they may glory in their illicit rule, for, like Turkish pashas, they hold more real power than their masters. But virtue is sacrificed to passing gratifications, and the respectability of a lifetime to the triumph of an hour.

Women, like despots, perhaps now have more power than they would have if the world, divided and subdivided into kingdoms and families, were governed by laws derived from the exercise of reason; but, to continue the comparison, in gaining that power they degrade their character, and licentiousness spreads through the whole of society. The many become a pedestal for the few. I will therefore venture to assert that until women are educated more rationally, the progress of human virtue and the advance of knowledge must be continually held back. And if it is granted that woman was not created merely to gratify man’s appetite, or to be the upper servant who provides his meals and looks after his linen, it follows that the first concern of those mothers or fathers who genuinely attend to the education of girls should be, if not to strengthen the body, then at least not to ruin the constitution with mistaken notions of beauty and female excellence. Nor should girls ever be allowed to absorb the harmful idea that a defect can, by some chemical process of reasoning, turn into an excellence. On this point I am glad to find that the author of one of the most instructive books our country has produced for children agrees with me; I shall quote his apt remarks, so that the force of his respected authority may support reason.*

(*Footnote. A respected old man gives the following sensible account of the method he followed in educating his daughter. “I endeavoured to give both to her mind and body a degree of vigour, which is seldom found in the female sex. As soon as she was sufficiently advanced in strength to be capable of the lighter labours of husbandry and gardening, I employed her as my constant companion. Selene, for that was her name, soon acquired a dexterity in all these rustic employments which I considered with equal pleasure and admiration. If women are in general feeble both in body and mind, it arises less from nature than from education. We encourage a vicious indolence and inactivity, which we falsely call delicacy; instead of hardening their minds by the severer principles of reason and philosophy, we breed them to useless arts, which terminate in vanity and sensuality. In most of the countries which I had visited, they are taught nothing of an higher nature than a few modulations of the voice, or useless postures of the body; their time is consumed in sloth or trifles, and trifles become the only pursuits capable of interesting them. We seem to forget, that it is upon the qualities of the female sex, that our own domestic comforts and the education of our children must depend. And what are the comforts or the education which a race of beings corrupted from their infancy, and unacquainted with all the duties of life, are fitted to bestow? To touch a musical instrument with useless skill, to exhibit their natural or affected graces, to the eyes of indolent and debauched young men, who dissipate their husbands’ patrimony in riotous and unnecessary expenses: these are the only arts cultivated by women in most of the polished nations I had seen. And the consequences are uniformly such as may be expected to proceed from such polluted sources, private misery, and public servitude.

“But, Selene’s education was regulated by different views, and conducted upon severer principles; if that can be called severity which opens the mind to a sense of moral and religious duties, and most effectually arms it against the inevitable evils of life.” — Mr. Day’s “Sandford and Merton,” Volume 3.)

But even if it were proved that woman is naturally weaker than man, how does it follow that it is natural for her to strive to become weaker still than nature meant her to be? Arguments of this kind insult common sense and smack of passion. In this enlightened age, one may hope, the DIVINE RIGHT of husbands, like the divine right of kings, can be challenged without danger; and though conviction may not silence many noisy disputants, whenever a prevailing prejudice is attacked the wise will reflect on it, and leave the narrow-minded to rail with thoughtless vehemence against innovation.

A mother who wishes to give her daughter true dignity of character must ignore the sneers of ignorance and follow a plan diametrically opposed to the one that Rousseau has recommended with all the beguiling charms of eloquence and philosophical sophistry; for his eloquence makes absurdities look plausible, and his dogmatic conclusions bewilder, without convincing, those who lack the ability to refute them.

Throughout the animal kingdom every young creature needs almost constant exercise, and, following this hint, children should spend their infancy in harmless romping that exercises the feet and hands without demanding close direction from the head or the constant attention of a nurse. Indeed, the care needed for self-preservation is the first natural exercise of the understanding, just as little inventions to amuse the passing moment unfold the imagination. But these wise designs of nature are defeated by misguided doting or blind zeal. The child — a girl especially — is not left to its own direction for a single moment, and is thus made dependent; and then dependence is called natural.

To preserve personal beauty — woman’s glory! — the limbs and faculties are cramped by worse than Chinese bindings, and the sedentary life girls are condemned to lead, while boys frolic in the open air, weakens their muscles and slackens their nerves. As for Rousseau’s remarks, since echoed by several writers, that girls naturally — that is, from birth and independently of education — love dolls, dressing up and talking, they are too childish to deserve serious refutation. It is indeed very natural that a girl condemned to sit for hours on end listening to the idle chatter of weak-minded nurses, or to wait on her mother while she dresses, should try to join in the conversation; and it is undoubtedly a most natural consequence that she should imitate her mother or aunts and amuse herself by decking out her lifeless doll just as they deck her out, poor innocent baby! For even men of the greatest abilities have seldom had strength enough to rise above the atmosphere around them; and if the page of genius has always been blurred by the prejudices of its age, some allowance should be made for a sex that, like kings, always sees things through a distorting medium.
